analysis.one_liner: Extends HIPAA-style privacy protections to health data held by apps, wearables, and data brokers.
analysis.headline: The Senate health committee approved the bill favorably in August 2026 and placed it on the Senate calendar, but no floor vote has been held.
analysis.plain_summary: Today's federal health privacy law (HIPAA) covers hospitals, insurers, and their contractors — but not the many companies outside the health system that collect health data: period-tracking apps, fitness wearables, health websites, and data brokers who buy and sell it. The bill directs HHS and the FTC to write rules, within 18 months, giving people control over that data: companies would need written permission to sell or market it, could not pass it to the government without a warrant or subpoena, could not keep it longer than needed, and could not use it to investigate someone for seeking health care. It also sets stricter national standards for 'de-identified' data and makes re-identifying it a punishable violation.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone whose health information lives outside a hospital or insurance company — users of fitness trackers, period and symptom apps, telehealth services, and health-related websites. The bill gives them rights they currently lack: notice, access, deletion within 30 days, portability between apps, breach notification, and consent before their data is sold. It also protects the privacy of people seeking sensitive care, since companies could not hand health data to the government without compulsory legal process.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Users of health apps and wearables

how_it_helps.text: Companies that determine how health data is used (including data brokers) must follow privacy, security, and breach-notification rules at least as strong as HIPAA's.

Selling, licensing, transferring, or marketing a person's health data requires that person's written authorization, and companies may not keep data longer than needed or collect beyond a HIPAA-style 'minimum necessary' limit.
Companies may not sell or transfer health data to any government entity except when compelled by warrant, subpoena, or court order.
The rules may not authorize using health data to investigate or impose liability on someone for seeking, obtaining, providing, or facilitating health care.
Individuals gain rights to notice, access, amendment, deletion (within 30 days), and portability of their health data, including precise location data that reveals they sought a health service.

HHS must set a single national de-identification standard stricter than current practice — ruling out the loose 'safe harbor' method, requiring contracts not to re-identify data, and accounting for AI-driven re-identification — with violations subject to civil penalties.
Apps generating wellness data (step counts, medication compliance) must tell users in plain language that the data is not HIPAA-protected and offer an opt-out before collecting it.

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers, digital health and wellness app companies, and advertisers who currently buy, sell, and target people using health data outside HIPAA. They face compliance costs, consent requirements, and restrictions on selling data or handing it to law enforcement voluntarily. Health providers and insurers, already covered by HIPAA, see little change.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers and health app companies

drawbacks.text: The bill applies HIPAA's preemption rule to its new requirements, which could override stricter state health-privacy laws in states that have gone further than federal law.
Enforcement rests with HHS and the FTC through civil penalties; the text provides no private right of action, so individuals could not sue violators themselves.
Protections arrive slowly: regulations are due 18 months after enactment and de-identification standards after a year, leaving the current gap in protection open in the meantime.
Compliance costs for app makers and data companies may be passed to consumers, and a national floor could reduce the regulatory patchwork some firms actually prefer to navigate state by state.

The bill preserves a rule allowing providers to charge fees, under state law, when transmitting records to certain third parties an individual designates, which can add cost to moving one's own records.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people the bill closes a real and growing hole: HIPAA simply does not cover most consumer health apps and data brokers, so health data collected outside a doctor's office can currently be sold with little restriction. The main honest concerns are that preemption could undo stronger state laws, that there is no right to sue, and that rulemaking delays mean protection is years away even if it passes. The core privacy gains outweigh the compliance costs, which fall mainly on firms profiting from the current gap.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate health committee approved it and placed it on the Senate's waiting list for floor business, but no vote has been scheduled with the session ending in January 2027.

narrative.text: Sen. Bill Cassidy introduced the bill on November 4, 2025, and it was read twice and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
On July 30, 2026, the HELP Committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, and it was reported on August 4, 2026.

The committee substitute strengthened the bill relative to the version introduced: it changed the standard from 'commensurate with' to 'at least equivalent to' HIPAA protections, added a ban on using health data to investigate someone for obtaining health care, added precise health-related geolocation to the covered data, explicitly covered data brokers, required written authorization for any sale or marketing of health data, barred transfers to government without compulsory process, and tightened the de-identification standard.
On August 4, 2026, the bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 538, where it awaits floor time.
No floor vote, amendment, or further Senate action has occurred since it was placed on the calendar, and the 119th Congress ends January 3, 2027.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far the bill has moved steadily toward the floor, which favors consumers; but until a vote happens, data brokers, wellness apps, and advertisers continue operating under the current looser rules, which they benefit from every day the bill waits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data brokers and ad-tech, for now

for.what_they_did: Ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute on July 30, 2026.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has a Republican sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor and cleared committee without a recorded floor vote, so no party split is visible in the record yet.

industries.note: The bill defines data brokers as regulated entities and requires their written authorization to sell health data, bars them from transferring it to governments without compulsory process, and subjects them to breach and minimization rules. Their current business model of trading health data collected from other sources would be directly restricted.

industries.industry: Digital health and wellness app makers
industries.note: They must obtain authorization to sell or market user health data, offer opt-outs for wellness data collection, honor deletion within 30 days, and meet security and breach rules — real compliance costs. But a single national standard replacing a patchwork of state laws can simplify operations, which is why the effect is not purely negative.

Precise geolocation showing that someone sought a health service becomes covered health data, and uses without written authorization are restricted, cutting off targeting of consumers based on sensitive health signals.

industries.industry: AI and machine learning developers using health data
industries.note: HHS must write rules on how the minimum-necessary standard applies to training AI models, and de-identification gets stricter with a penalty for re-identification — limiting access to the large health datasets these firms want. Research and interoperability pathways are preserved, so access is narrowed rather than eliminated.

As HIPAA covered entities and business associates they are largely carved out of the new regime for protected health information, though the bill retains a provision letting providers charge fees to third parties when transmitting a patient's records at the patient's direction.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits on the Senate calendar with favorable bipartisan committee action but no scheduled floor time and a session ending January 3, 2027. Bills at this stage typically die at adjournment unless leadership allocates floor time or the bill is folded into a larger package, such as a health or data-privacy vehicle; without a visible coalition of senators pressing for time, passage odds are low.
